hooks.text: A two-hundred-foot asteroid flew past Earth before anyone saw it.
How did a two-hundred-foot asteroid slip past every space telescope?
A city-killing asteroid swept past Earth, and nobody noticed.

title: The City-Killer Hiding in the Sun
description: In July 2023, a 200-foot asteroid swept past Earth completely undetected because it approached directly out of the solar glare. Early warning telescopes only spotted it two days after its closest approach.

beats.text: A two-hundred-foot asteroid flew past Earth before anyone saw it.
beats.visual: Artist concept of a near-Earth asteroid approaching Earth

beats.text: Most people believe space telescopes track every city-killing rock near our planet.
beats.visual: Panoramic view of astronomical telescopes under night sky

beats.text: But on July 13, 2023, asteroid 2023 NT1 swept past at one-quarter of the distance to the Moon.
beats.visual: Diagram showing the orbit of asteroid 2023 NT1 past Earth and Moon

beats.text: Approaching directly out of the Sun's blinding glare, the rock stayed completely hidden.
beats.visual: Solar corona and intense glare observed by SOHO space observatory

beats.text: Two days after it passed, an ATLAS observatory telescope in South Africa finally spotted it.
beats.visual: Dome of the ATLAS observatory telescope in Sutherland South Africa

beats.text: The Chelyabinsk meteor used this exact solar blind spot in 2013, injuring roughly fifteen hundred people.
beats.visual: Smoke trail of the Chelyabinsk meteor across the Russian sky in 2013

beats.text: To catch these blind-spot hazards, the European Space Agency is developing the NEOMIR spacecraft to launch around 2030.
beats.visual: Artist impression of ESA NEOMIR satellite at Sun-Earth L1 point
queries: Sun Earth L1 Lagrange point diagram

beats.text: Without satellites monitoring the Sun, solar glare can still blind our early warning systems.
beats.visual: Diagram of Sun-Earth Lagrange points showing solar observation orbit
